metadata.title: Numeracy practices and numeracy skills among adults (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The report uses microdata from the Survey of Adult Skills (PIAAC) conducted in 33 countries/economies, with respondents completing a biographical questionnaire and numeracy assessment (and problem-solving in technology-rich environments for 28 countries). The analyses are based on a restricted set of 30 countries/economies (excluding Cyprus, Jakarta, and the Russian Federation) and further restrict the analytic population by labour-force status (e.g., employed-only for workplace analyses; excluding students for some everyday-practice items). The report does not specify the exact sampling/replicate weight variables in the provided text, so analysts should consult the PIAAC technical documentation for the appropriate student/sampling weights and replicate weights for variance estimation. If weights are not applied, results should be interpreted as descriptive/associational rather than fully population-representative estimates under the complex survey design.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The report’s outcomes are primarily derived from PIAAC numeracy proficiency scores and self-reported practice indices constructed from questionnaire items, but the provided text does not document a specific plausible-values (PV) workflow (e.g., Rubin’s rules) or a concrete missing-data strategy for the analytic models. Missingness is discussed descriptively (e.g., “% Missing” in practice items) and some countries are excluded due to missing-answer proportions or coverage limitations, but the text does not state whether missing responses were handled via listwise deletion, imputation, or other methods in the regression/causal-path analyses. This is therefore a reporting gap for missing-data handling at the model-estimation stage.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Analyses are based on PIAAC data from 30 of the 33 participating countries/economies in the first two rounds. The report explicitly excludes Cyprus (due to a high proportion of missing answers due to language problems), Jakarta (because the assessment was carried out exclusively on paper), and the Russian Federation (because of incomplete coverage of the Russian population). For some chapters/analyses, the analytic population is further restricted to employed adults (workplace numeracy-practice analyses) and, for certain everyday financial-practice items, students are excluded.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD working paper analyzes the relationship between adult numeracy proficiency and the frequency/intensity of numeracy practices in everyday life and at work using PIAAC microdata. The report constructs an “intensity of engagement” index from eight ordinal questionnaire items on numeracy-related activities, using a two-parameter IRT approach to place individuals on a 0–1 scale and then classify engagement into three groups (limited, median, intensive). Numeracy proficiency is measured via a direct numeracy assessment reported on a 0–500 scale with proficiency levels (1–5 plus below 1). The analyses compare students vs non-students and examine how individual characteristics (e.g., age, gender, education, numeracy/literacy proficiency) and job characteristics relate to engagement, and how engagement relates to proficiency, employability, wages, and well-being (e.g., health). The report emphasizes “use it or lose it” patterns but does not provide a documented ML prediction pipeline; results are associational and may not identify causal direction.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is an OECD report using PIAAC to describe and model associations between numeracy proficiency and numeracy practices across countries and subpopulations. The provided text does not document an ML predictive modeling workflow (no ML algorithms, no train/test evaluation metrics), so main_findings and confounders_identified are left empty per the schema rules for non-ML report extractions. Several fields (e.g., total sample size and per-country Ns) are not reported in the excerpt, and the report also does not specify PV and missing-data handling procedures in the provided text, which limits extraction granularity.
